docs.title: Grounding rationale (LOF-P-004)
docs.text:
• Periods are temporal regions, not processes. Being in force is not something that happens; it is a standing condition that holds through a region of time. The pattern therefore relates content to BFO temporal regions instead of reifying a "force" entity. Entry into force is the first instant of such a region, a BFO temporal instant.
  • Calendar values on instants, not regions. BFO already relates a region to its first and last instants. Putting the date-time on the instant keeps one value per entity, makes an instant reusable as the bound of several regions (the last instant of a compliance period is also what triggers the power to fine), and matches OWL-Time, where time:inXSDDateTimeStamp sits on time:Instant.
  • Amendment as succession of content. Legal content is a generically dependent continuant (ODP-001). Treating amendment as the establishment of new content that succeeds the old, rather than as a change in old content, keeps every version citable as it stood and avoids ascribing change to an abstract pattern.
  • Consolidated version as generically dependent continuant. A consolidation is information content about the law. It is not declared disjoint from legal content, so that an enacted consolidation can be asserted to be both (LOF-P-010). It has its own period, because it stops stating the law at the next amendment while the base content stays in force.
  • Compliance period as a defined temporal region. No new primitive: a region is a compliance period by being the period some position is due within.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The GDPR, the Directive it repealed, and the United Kingdom Act that transposed the Directive, with real dates; and a hypothetical controller that notifies one breach late and one in time. Excerpt:

ex:gdprEnactment a odp1:0001003 ;            # enactment
    odp1:0001100 ex:gdpr ;                   # establishes
    odp5:0001101 ex:directive9546 .          # repeals (Art. 94(1)), with effect from 25 May 2018
ex:dpa1998Enactment a odp1:0001003 ;
    odp1:0001100 ex:dpa1998 ;
    odp1:0001102 ex:directive9546 .          # performed under: transposition

ex:gdpr odp5:0001102 ex:gdprInForce ;        # in force during (Art. 99(1))
        odp5:0001103 ex:gdprApplies ;        # applies during (Art. 99(2))
        odp5:0001108 ex:directive9546 .      # succeeds
ex:directive9546 odp5:0001102 ex:directiveInForce .   # in force, never applying to private processing
ex:dpa1998 odp5:0001102 ex:dpaInForce ; odp5:0001103 ex:dpaInForce .

ex:gdprApplies obo:BFO_0000222 ex:t20180525 .          # has first instant
ex:t20180525 odp5:0001200 "2018-05-24T22:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTimeStamp .   # 25 May 2018, 00:00 Brussels

ex:window1 odp5:0001107 ex:awareness1 ;      # computed from (aware at 08:40)
    obo:BFO_0000222 ex:window1Start ;        # 09:00: Reg. 1182/71 Art. 3 excludes the starting hour
    obo:BFO_0000224 ex:window1End .          # 5 March 2026, 08:59:59 UTC
ex:notifyDuty1 a odp3:0001002 ;              # duty (Art. 33(1))
    odp5:0001106 ex:window1 ;                # due within
    odp4:0001106 ex:window1 .                # undischarged during
ex:finePower1 a odp3:0001005 ;               # power (Art. 83(4)(a))
    odp4:0001102 ex:window1End .             # triggered by the end of the period

Inferred by HermiT, under both ODP-003 options: the adoption of the GDPR is a repeal and so an amending act; both seventy-two-hour windows are compliance periods.

Question Answer from the example In force on 15 March 2017 Directive 95/46/EC, the Data Protection Act 1998, and the GDPR Applies to processing in March 2017 the Data Protection Act 1998; the Directive and the GDPR are in force but do not apply to it Repealed, succeeded, force ended Directive 95/46/EC, by the adoption of the GDPR, succeeded by the GDPR, end of 24 May 2018 Consolidation text 02016R0679-20160504 combines the GDPR and states the law from 24 May 2016 Overdue Acme's duty to notify breach 1, due by 5 March 2026 08:59:59 UTC, computed from its awareness of the breach; the end of the period triggers the authority's power to fine

Two points the example makes explicit. Article 33(1) requires notification "without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours"; the compliance period records the fixed limit, and whether a later notification with reasons was lawful is for the rule layer. And the fine of Article 83 is a sanction, not a remedy in the ODP-004 sense of making good the failure, so the power is linked by what triggers it, not by remedies (open question 5).

The example also contains a period that ends before it begins, which the shapes report as a violation. The full example is src/examples/gdpr-timeline.ttl.

ELI and Akoma Ntoso record these facts about documents and their expressions. This pattern records them about legal content, so that a period of force can be related to the positions grounded in that content and to the chain of ODP-004.

docs.title: Consequences and limitations
docs.text:
• Instance level only. The pattern records that a particular period was computed from a particular occurrence. The rule "seventy-two hours after becoming aware" is type-level and belongs to a rule layer, as in ODP-004.
  • No interval reasoning in OWL. OWL cannot compare date-time values within class definitions, so "in force at t" and "overdue" are answered by SPARQL, and period well-formedness by SHACL. The pattern deliberately does not import OWL-Time's interval algebra, which would add Allen relations the queries do not need.
  • Suspension and revival are represented as several in force during regions for the same content; the gap between them is the suspension.
  • No discharge relation. The pattern says a position is due within a period and, with ODP-004, that it went undischarged during it. It does not link a position to the process that discharged it (open question 3).
  • Repeal is not the only end of force. A sunset clause, implied repeal, desuetude, or annulment ends force with no repealing act; the pattern records them by the last instant of the region in force alone, so CQ3 sees only repeals made by acts.
  • One time line. The pattern records the periods as now understood. When a court annuls content ex tunc, the content was in force as people then believed and is treated as never in force afterwards. Recording both requires a second, transaction-time dimension (open question 6).
  • Jurisdiction. Nothing in the pattern assumes the European Union. It has been checked against the forms below, all of which it can express (LOF-P-010):
Form How it is expressed Delayed application (GDPR) in force during and applies during with different first instants Retroactivity applies during a region that begins before the in force during region Sunset clause an in force during region whose last instant is set by the enacting content Repeal with saving provision in force during ends; applies during continues for facts before the repeal Suspension, revival two in force during regions Directive and transposition the directive in force during only; the transposing content applies during, its enactment performed under the directive (ODP-001) Positive-law codification (US Code) a consolidated version asserted also to be legal content established by an enactment Annulment by a court the last instant of the region in force, with no repealing act

docs.title: Open questions for the founding coordinators
docs.text:
1. Amendment target. Amends relates an act to the content it amends, following ODP-001, and succeeds relates the texts. Should amended by (content to act) also be provided, or is the inverse enough?
  2. Limitation periods and other periods for second-order positions. A limitation period, or a time to appeal, is a period within which a power may be exercised, not one within which a position must be discharged. Due within does not cover it. Should there be a parallel exercisable within for powers, here or in ODP-004?
  3. Discharge. Should a relation from a position to the process that discharged it (discharged by) be added here, in ODP-004, or in a compliance pattern of its own?
  4. Versions of positions. When content is succeeded, are the positions it grounds ended and replaced, or do they persist? Under ODP-003 Option A they are replaced; under Option B they may persist. The pattern takes no position, and the example does not depend on it.
  5. Sanctions. A fine is not a remedy in the ODP-004 sense. Should ODP-004 distinguish sanctions (powers whose exercise penalizes the failure) from remedies (positions that make it good), with sanctioning positions linked to the failure they penalize?
  6. Bitemporality. Annulment ex tunc (and the Akoma Ntoso treatment of unconstitutionality) needs a record of what was believed in force at a time as well as what is now held to have been in force. Should the Foundry add a transaction-time layer, or leave it to the data store?
  7. Instants as triggers. The end of a compliance period triggers the power to fine. ODP-004 triggered by has the range occurrent, and a BFO instant is a temporal region, an occurrent, so this is valid; should ODP-004 say so explicitly?

docs.title: LOF-ODP-006: Relations between Norms
docs.text:
Identifier LOF-ODP-006 IRI https://w3id.org/lof/odp-006.owl Repository https://github.com/legal-ontologies-foundry/lof-odp-006 Status draft Version 0.1.0 Depends on LOF-ODP-001, LOF-ODP-003 Drafted by David R. Koepsell For review by William Mandrick, Barry Smith

Draft for review

First draft, prepared for discussion by the founding coordinators. Open questions are listed at the end.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Legal content rarely stands alone. A national statute fills in what a regulation leaves open; a research exemption, permitted by the regulation itself, removes cases from a right of access; a specific consent rule displaces a general legal basis; a municipal ordinance collides with a regulation of higher rank. To answer what the law requires of someone, one has to know which content bears on which, which items conflict, and which prevails, on what ground, and on whose authority.

This pattern provides those relations. It treats conflict as a relation between the legal positions two items of content ground, which is where incompatibility actually lies, and infers conflict between the content from it. It treats a statement that one item prevails over another as an entity in its own right, because it has three parts that matter (which prevails, which yields, on what ground) and a source whose authority may differ: a conflict rule in the legislation, a court's holding, or guidance with no legal force. The pattern keeps those apart: any determination makes one content held to prevail over another, but only a determination that is itself legal content makes it prevail over it. And it keeps open the cases the law leaves open: a conflict that nothing resolves, and one on which authorities disagree, are reported, not hidden.

docs.title: Competency questions
docs.text:
1. Which provisions particularize, derogate from, or create exceptions to which, and under what content was the act containing them enacted?
  2. Which items of legal content conflict, through which positions, held by whom?
  3. For each determination, which content prevails, on what ground, according to whom, and does the determination have legal force?
  4. What is the status of each conflict: settled with legal force, held only by readings without force, contested, or unresolved?

All four are answered by SPARQL (src/sparql/); unresolved, contested, and unauthoritatively resolved conflicts are also reported by the SHACL shapes (src/shapes/).

docs.text:
Label IRI BFO parent Definition priority principle ODP006_0001000 generically dependent continuant A generically dependent continuant that states, on some ground such as rank, specificity, or time, which of two conflicting items of legal content prevails. precedence determination ODP006_0001001 generically dependent continuant A generically dependent continuant that states that one item of legal content prevails over another where they conflict. authoritative precedence determination ODP006_0001002 precedence determination (defined) A precedence determination that is itself legal content.

Four priority principles are provided as individuals: lex superior (ODP006_0001500), lex specialis (ODP006_0001501), lex posterior (ODP006_0001502), and primacy of an overriding legal order (ODP006_0001503). The last covers any regime in which the content of one legal order prevails over conflicting content of another: European Union law over national law (Case 6/64 Costa v ENEL), federal law over state law in the United States (Constitution Article VI, clause 2), federal paramountcy in Canada, section 109 of the Australian Constitution, and the Charter of the United Nations over other treaty obligations (Article 103). It is kept apart from lex superior, which ranks content within a single legal order, because it relates two orders, and its effect on the yielding content varies by regime: set aside in the case under EU law (Case 106/77 Simmenthal), without effect or inoperative under US preemption and Canadian paramountcy, invalid to the extent of the inconsistency in Australia. The pattern does not fix that effect (see open question 1). A regime-specific variant that needs its own identity can be added as a further individual with dcterms:coverage naming the regime. Lex posterior compares the enactments that established the content (ODP-001), not their dates of entry into force; where a system uses another date, record the choice.

docs.text:

The first chain lifts conflict from positions to the content that grounds them. The second makes held to prevail over the shadow of every determination. The last three do the same for prevails over, but only for determinations asserted to be legal content: the self-link, which holds of an individual exactly when it is an authoritative determination, carries the class into the property chain. Authoritatively favours is not declared a subproperty of favours, because a chain-defined property cannot be a subproperty of a property in its own chain without making the hierarchy irregular, which OWL 2 DL forbids.

Derogation does not imply precedence. An earlier draft made derogates from a subproperty of prevails over. That made BDSG section 27(2) prevail over the GDPR, which is wrong: the German provision restricts the right of access only because GDPR Article 89(2) permits it, and if the two truly conflicted, the GDPR would prevail. The authorization is now recorded with ODP-001: the enactment of the derogating content is performed under the content that permits it.

docs.title: Grounding rationale (LOF-P-004)
docs.text:
• Conflict lies between positions. Two texts are not incompatible as texts; they are incompatible because no one can comply with both, or because one permits what the other forbids. That is a fact about the positions they ground (ODP-003), held by particular parties. Locating conflict there makes it precise (whose positions, held by whom) and makes the content-level relation derivable rather than stipulated.
  • Determinations are information content. That one provision prevails over another is stated somewhere and can be stated differently elsewhere. It is therefore a generically dependent continuant, for the reason legal content is (ODP-001): the same determination is borne by a judgment, a commentary, and a database record. The act of determining is a process; the determination is what it yields. It is asserted to be legal content as well when its source makes it so (a conflict rule in a statute, a court's holding), and is then classified as authoritative.
  • Force is a property of the determination, not of the relation. Whether A prevails over B in law depends on who said so. Deriving prevails over from authoritative determinations only, and held to prevail over from all of them, lets guidance, scholarship, and annotation be recorded without being mistaken for law.
  • Priority principles are not declared legal content. Lex specialis and lex posterior are codified in some systems (for example the Italian preleggi) and doctrinal in others. Declaring them legal content would build one tradition into the pattern (LOF-P-010).
  • No new primitives for derogation. Derogation and specification are relations between items of ODP-001 legal content. Their scope (which cases) is type-level and is left to the rule layer.

docs.text:
From the GDPR's neighbourhood, with real provisions and a hypothetical shop, municipality, and court. Excerpt:

    odp6:0001108 odp6:0001503 ;                  # primacy of an overriding legal order (EU law)

Inferred by HermiT, under both ODP-003 options:

Content Inferred relation Content From ePrivacy Art. 5(3); TDDDG s. 25 content conflicts with, held to prevail over GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) the conflicting positions; Recital 173 and EDPB Opinion 5/2019, lex specialis, neither with legal force GDPR Art. 9(1) content conflicts with, held to prevail over, prevails over municipal ordinance (hypothetical) the conflicting duties; an annotator's reading and a court's holding (hypothetical), primacy of an overriding legal order (EU law) BDSG s. 27(2) creates exception to, and nothing more GDPR Art. 15 the derogation; the BDSG enactment is performed under Art. 89(2)

The court's determination is classified as an authoritative precedence determination because it is asserted to be legal content; the annotator's, Recital 173's, and the EDPB's are not.

Section 26(2) is used rather than section 26(1) because the validity of 26(1) as an Article 88 rule is doubtful after Case C-34/21 (Hauptpersonalrat, 30 March 2023), which held that a national rule merely restating the GDPR is not one.

The example also contains two deliberate defects. Provisions A and B ground conflicting duties and nothing resolves them: the shapes report an unresolved conflict (a warning). Two readings disagree on whether C or D prevails: the shapes report contested precedence (a warning), and CQ4 reports the conflict as contested. The cookie conflict is reported as resolved only by determinations without legal force (information). The full example is src/examples/gdpr-norm-relations.ttl.

This pattern LOMO LegalRuleML Akoma Ntoso LKIF-Core particularizes lomo:specifies, close match none none none derogates from lomo:derogatesFrom, close match lrml:Override, partial scopeMod, related none substitutes for / creates exception to substitutive and blocking derogation, described in LOMO's documentation only (no properties) defeaters, partial exceptionOfScope, close match for exception none conflicts with none (conflict represented only once resolved) none at the instance level none none held to prevail over none lrml:Override, related none none prevails over none lrml:Override (over, under), close match none none precedence determination, priority principle none none none none

The mappings are also published as SSSOM in src/mappings/odp-006-standards.sssom.tsv.

LegalRuleML expresses defeasible priority among rules for a reasoner, at the type level. This pattern records, at the instance level, that a particular conflict exists and how and by whom it was resolved. A LegalRuleML rule base can be generated from the determinations, and its conclusions recorded back as determinations.

docs.title: Consequences and limitations
docs.text:
• Conflict is asserted. Whether two positions conflict depends on the conduct they concern, which is the action-type problem of ODP-003 open question 2. Until that is solved, conflict between positions is asserted by the annotator, and only conflict between content is inferred.
  • No scope. Derogation and specification hold "for the cases within its scope". The scope is not represented, so the pattern cannot say for which facts the derogating content governs. That belongs to the rule layer.
  • Open world. OWL can infer that a conflict is resolved but not that it is unresolved, since a determination may simply be unrecorded. Unresolved conflicts are reported by SHACL on a reasoned graph.
  • No asymmetry axiom, and cycles are not errors. OWL 2 DL forbids declaring a property defined by a chain asymmetric, so mutual precedence is not an inconsistency. It is reported by SHACL as contested (a warning), because it can be the law's real state: courts of two legal orders can each hold, with authority in their own order, that their law prevails (compare the Court of Justice and the German Federal Constitutional Court in the PSPP case, 2 BvR 859/15, 5 May 2020).
  • Not transitive. Precedence is not transitive across different scopes (A over B for employees, B over C for contractors says nothing of A and C), so neither precedence relation is declared transitive.
  • Other precedence regimes. Federal preemption (including field preemption), UN Charter Article 103, Article 30 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, and precedence clauses in contracts all have the shape of a priority principle; they are not provided as individuals, and can be added with their own coverage.
  • Lex posterior needs dates. The pattern does not compare dates. With LOF-ODP-001 enactments placed in time by LOF-ODP-005, a SPARQL check can confirm that content favoured on the ground of lex posterior was enacted after the content it displaces.

docs.title: Relation to A Structural Ontology of the Law
docs.text:
The typology of legal contradictions in Koepsell, A Structural Ontology of the Law (Palgrave Macmillan, forthcoming) classifies conflicts by the link of the Minimum Legal Chain at which they arise. This pattern supplies only what such a typology needs from the Foundry: conflicts located at legal positions, with their content, holders, and resolution status. The typology itself is theory-specific and is left out, consistent with LOF-P-008 and LOF-P-009, as in ODP-004.

Declaration of interest. The drafter is the author of that book.

docs.title: Open questions for the founding coordinators
docs.text:
1. What "prevails" means. The yielding content may be invalid (lex superior within one order), set aside or inoperative in the case (primacy of an overriding legal order, as with EU law), or merely displaced for the cases in scope (lex specialis). Should prevails over carry the effect, for example by subproperties, or should the effect be read from the priority principle?
  2. Conflict between positions of different holders. A duty of A to do X and a claim of B that A not do X are a conflict, though held by different parties. Should the pattern define the kinds of conflict (same holder, correlative pairs) or leave conflicts with general, as now?
  3. Who makes a determination authoritative. The pattern treats a determination as authoritative when it is asserted to be legal content. Should authority instead be relative to a legal order, so that the PSPP case is two authoritative holdings each with force in its own order?
  4. Priority among principles. Lex specialis and lex posterior can point in opposite directions (a later general rule against an earlier special one). Should the pattern represent second-order priority between principles, or leave that to the rule layer?
  5. Particularization and validity. The line between making content more determinate and displacing it is contested in EU law (Article 88 after C-34/21). Should particularizes carry a note that it does not certify the particularizing content's validity?

  • LOF-ODP-004 supplies the chain whose links a contradiction typology indexes; unresolved conflicts are its natural input.
  • LOF-ODP-005 places enactments in time for lex posterior and gives the periods during which a derogation is in force.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Gives legal content periods in force and periods of application (kept apart, since they come apart), records the acts that amend and repeal it, distinguishes consolidated versions from the law they consolidate, and gives legal positions compliance periods computed from the occurrences that start them, with region bounds as BFO instants carrying time-zoned date-times. With LOF-ODP-004, it identifies overdue positions. The full specification is on the pattern page.

docs.title: Deprecation policy
docs.text: Terms are never deleted (LOF-P-005). A term that should no longer be used is deprecated, following the same conventions as the OBO Foundry's obsoletion policy.

docs.title: When to deprecate
docs.text:
• The term's meaning must change. Deprecate it and mint a new term.
  • The term duplicates another term, in this or another member ontology (LOF-P-009).
  • The term was created in error, or is out of scope.

Changes to a label or a definition that do not change the term's meaning do not require deprecation.

docs.title: How to deprecate
docs.text:
1. Add owl:deprecated true.
  2. Prefix the label with obsolete (for example, "obsolete legal duty").
  3. Remove all logical axioms in which the term appears (subclass axioms, equivalences, restrictions), so it no longer affects reasoning.
  4. Add one of the following:
    • IAO:0100001 (term replaced by) pointing to the single replacement term, or
    • oboInOwl:consider pointing to one or more candidate terms, when there is no exact replacement.
  5. Add an rdfs:comment explaining why, with a link to the issue.
  6. Record the deprecation in CHANGELOG.md.

The automated check deprecated-without-replacement-violation enforces step 4.

docs.title: Deprecating an ontology
docs.text: An ontology that is no longer maintained or has been superseded is set to status: deprecated in the registry, with replaced_by naming its successor if there is one. Its identifiers and releases remain resolvable indefinitely.

docs.title: ID ranges
docs.text: To stop two editors from minting the same identifier, each editor of an ontology is allocated a range of seven-digit numbers. Allocations are recorded in src/ontology/lof-{id}-idranges.owl in the ontology's repository, in the format used by the OBO Foundry and the Ontology Development Kit.

docs.title: Default allocation
docs.text: Range Use 0000001 to 0000999 Reserved 0001000 to 0001999 First editor 0002000 to 0002999 Second editor 0003000 to 0003999 Third editor 0004000 and above Allocated on request

docs.title: Protégé setup
docs.text:
In Protégé, open Preferences > New Entities and set:

  • Entity IRI: Start with Specified IRI https://w3id.org/lof, Followed by /, End with Auto-generated ID.
  • Entity Label: Custom label, rdfs:label.
  • Auto-generated ID: Numeric (iterative), prefix {PREFIX}_, 7 digits, starting at the beginning of your range, and ending at its end.

To request a range, open an issue in the ontology's repository, or ask its contact person.

docs.title: Identifier policy
docs.text: All Foundry identifiers live in the persistent namespace https://w3id.org/lof/. The redirects are maintained in the w3id.org repository and generated from the registry, so hosting can change without breaking any identifier (LOF-P-005).

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
Kind Pattern Example Foundry home https://w3id.org/lof/ Full release (latest) https://w3id.org/lof/{id}.owl https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001.owl Base release (latest) https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/{id}-base.owl https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/odp-001-base.owl Specific release https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/releases/{version}/{id}.owl https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/releases/0.1.0/odp-001.owl Import module https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/imports/{file} https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/imports/bfo_import.owl Term https://w3id.org/lof/{PREFIX}_{7 digits} https://w3id.org/lof/ODP001_0001000 Issue tracker https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/tracker Home page https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/home

{id} is the lower-case registry identifier. {PREFIX} is the upper-case prefix reserved in the registry.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Local identifiers are opaque seven-digit numbers. They never encode labels.
  2. An identifier, once published in a release, is never reassigned and never deleted. See the deprecation policy.
  3. Each editor mints identifiers only from their allocated ID range.
  4. Prefixes are reserved when an ontology is registered at draft status and remain reserved even if it is deprecated.

docs.title: Term resolution
docs.text: Term IRIs currently redirect to the ontology's page in the registry. When a term browser is deployed (for example, an OLS or Ontobee instance), the term redirects will be updated to point at it, with no change to the IRIs.

docs.title: Registry metadata
docs.text:
Each ontology in the registry is described by one file, ontology/{id}.md, in the website repository. The file has YAML front matter holding the metadata, followed by a Markdown body holding a longer description. This is the same arrangement the OBO Foundry uses.

The front matter is validated against the JSON Schema in util/schema/registry_schema.json on every pull request. From these files the build generates:

  • the registry page and one page per ontology,
  • machine-readable registries at registry/ontologies.yml and registry/ontologies.jsonld,
  • the .htaccess redirects for w3id.org/lof.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Required Meaning id yes Lower-case identifier; must match the file name. preferred_prefix yes Upper-case prefix for term IRIs. title yes Full title. description yes One-sentence description. domain yes The part of legal reality covered. jurisdictions yes Jurisdictions or traditions in scope, or general (LOF-P-010). status yes draft, candidate, accepted, or deprecated. activity_status yes active, inactive, or orphaned. repository yes GitHub repository URL. tracker yes Issue tracker URL. license yes label and url. contact yes label, email, and github (LOF-P-017). homepage no Defaults to the repository. branch no Release branch; defaults to main. dependencies no List of ids: registry ids or bfo, ro, iao, cco. usages no List of description and optional url (LOF-P-016). publications no List of id (DOI or URL) and title. review no date and issue URL of the review that set the status. replaced_by no For deprecated ontologies, the successor's id.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: status Meaning draft Registered and under development. The prefix is reserved. candidate Submitted for review against the principles. accepted Reviewed and found to satisfy the principles. deprecated Superseded or no longer maintained. Identifiers remain resolvable. activity_status Meaning active Maintainers are responsive and releases are current. inactive No release or issue activity for 12 months. orphaned Maintainers have withdrawn; new maintainers sought.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

These principles are a founding draft, modeled on the OBO Foundry principles and adapted to the legal domain. They take effect when ratified by the founding coordinators under the rules in Governance.

Every member ontology commits to the following principles. Each has its own page setting out its purpose, requirements, implementation, and the criteria reviewers apply. Principle numbers are permanent and never reused, so reviews and discussions can cite them precisely (for example, "fails LOF-P-007").

Principles LOF-P-004 (explicit grounding of legal entities) and LOF-P-010 (jurisdictional transparency) have no direct OBO counterpart. They address problems specific to law.

ID Principle Summary LOF-P-001 Open The ontology is openly available and may be used by all without constraint other than attribution. LOF-P-002 Common format The ontology is released in OWL 2, with a stable primary release file. LOF-P-003 Common upper ontology The ontology is aligned to Basic Formal Ontology, and every class descends from a BFO class. LOF-P-004 Explicit grounding of legal entities Each top-level legal class states which BFO category it falls under, and why. LOF-P-005 Persistent identifiers Every entity has a persistent IRI in the https://w3id.org/lof/ namespace, and IRIs are never reassigned or deleted. LOF-P-006 Versioning Each release carries a version IRI and version number, and every earlier release remains resolvable. LOF-P-007 Textual definitions Every class and relation has a precise, non-circular textual definition. LOF-P-008 Clearly delineated scope The ontology has a stated scope and a set of competency questions. LOF-P-009 Orthogonality Member ontologies do not duplicate one another's content. LOF-P-010 Jurisdictional transparency Classes specific to a legal system or jurisdiction are marked as such and are not presented as universal. LOF-P-011 Logical well-formedness Each release is logically consistent and contains no unsatisfiable classes. LOF-P-012 Naming conventions Labels are unique, singular, and follow a consistent lexical style. LOF-P-013 Documentation The ontology has a public repository with documentation and an issue tracker. LOF-P-014 Responsiveness and maintenance Maintainers respond to issues and keep the ontology aligned with its dependencies. LOF-P-015 Alignment with existing legal standards The ontology documents its relationship to established legal information standards. LOF-P-016 Documented use The ontology has documented users, or a credible plan for use. LOF-P-017 Locus of authority Each ontology has a single named point of contact responsible for it. LOF-P-018 Attribution Contributors to the ontology are credited, and it can be cited.

Checks that can be automated are listed on the automated checks page.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license (CC BY 4.0), so that anyone may use it without constraint other than attribution.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal ontologies are infrastructure for courts, agencies, researchers, and developers across jurisdictions. Restrictive licenses fragment that infrastructure and prevent the integration the Foundry exists to support.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Every Foundry ontology is released under CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), the current version of the Creative Commons Attribution license. Attribution is what makes contributions creditable and citable (LOF-P-018).
  2. The license is declared in the ontology header with dcterms:license whose value is the license IRI.
  3. The same license is recorded in the ontology's registry metadata.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Add Annotation(dcterms:license <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>) to the ontology header. The ontology template does this by default.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The header of every file generated from the LOF ontology template declares CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
The ontology header and the registry entry both declare CC BY 4.0. Content derived from sources with incompatible licenses (for example, proprietary legal databases) is not included.

Automated check: ROBOT report check missing_ontology_license; registry schema validation of license.

Proposed for adoption

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology is released in OWL 2, with a stable primary release file.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A common format lets member ontologies import one another and lets the same tools (Protégé, ROBOT, reasoners, triple stores) operate on all of them.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. A release file lof-{id}.owl is published at the root of the ontology repository, serialized as RDF/XML or Turtle.
  2. A base file lof-{id}-base.owl, containing only the ontology's own axioms, is also published.
  3. Other serializations may be offered, but the OWL release is authoritative.
  4. A new release is made whenever the ontology changes in a way its users should see (new or changed terms, definitions, or axioms), and at least once every 12 months while the ontology is active. An ontology with no release in 12 months is recorded as inactive (metadata policy).

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Run make release VERSION=x.y.z in src/ontology/. The template Makefile produces both files with ROBOT.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001.owl (full) and https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/odp-001-base.owl (base).

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Both release files exist, parse without error, and resolve through their persistent IRIs. The latest release is no more than 12 months old, or the ontology is recorded as inactive.

Automated check: CI parse and merge with ROBOT on every push.

docs.title: LOF-P-003: Common upper ontology
docs.text:
Proposed for adoption

This principle is part of a proposal for adoption, Adopt principles: grounding and logic (#55), which is not yet open for decision. Comments are welcome now, from anyone. When it opens, members will be able to approve or object here.

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology is aligned to Basic Formal Ontology, and every class descends from a BFO class, by assertion or by inference.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A shared upper ontology is what makes independently developed ontologies interoperable. It guarantees that an obligation modeled in one ontology and a role modeled in another stand in well-defined relations to each other and to the physical and documentary entities they depend on.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. The ontology imports BFO 2020 (ISO/IEC 21838-2), or a module extracted from it.
  2. Every class in the ontology is a subclass, directly or through its ancestors, of a BFO class. For a defined class (one given by an equivalence axiom, such as conferred legal role in LOF-ODP-002), the BFO ancestor may be inferred rather than asserted: its definition must have a genus, a named class that itself descends from BFO, so that a reasoner places the defined class under BFO. A defined class with no such genus (for example, a union of classes from different BFO categories) is not allowed.
  3. BFO relations are used wherever they carry the intended meaning. Relations from the Relation Ontology (RO) or from other member ontologies are reused before new relations are minted.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The template imports BFO 2020 core through src/ontology/imports/bfo_import.owl. Refresh it with make imports.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A class legal role declared as a subclass of BFO role (BFO:0000023).

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
No class lacks a BFO ancestor in the reasoned ontology. New relations are justified against existing BFO and RO relations.

Automated check: SPARQL check not-bfo-grounded-violation, run on the ontology after reasoning, so that defined classes are checked against their inferred ancestors.

docs.title: LOF-P-004: Explicit grounding of legal entities
docs.text:
Proposed for adoption

This principle is part of a proposal for adoption, Adopt principles: grounding and logic (#55), which is not yet open for decision. Comments are welcome now, from anyone. When it opens, members will be able to approve or object here.

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Each top-level legal class states which BFO category it falls under, and why.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal entities such as obligations, rights, powers, legal persons, institutions, legal acts, and legal documents do not fit naive physical categories, and reasonable ontologists disagree about their placement. The Foundry does not settle every such dispute by fiat. It requires that each ontology make its choice explicit and defend it, so that alignment across ontologies is possible and disagreements are visible rather than hidden.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Each top-level legal class (a class whose parent is a BFO class) has an rdfs:comment or linked documentation stating the rationale for its BFO placement.
  2. Where a Foundry design pattern (LOF-ODP) covers the modeling problem, the ontology uses it or documents why it departs from it.
  3. Placements that conflict with an accepted member ontology are raised with the Editorial Working Group before release.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Record the rationale in the class annotation, and summarize the grounding decisions in a section of the ontology's README.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Legal obligation placed under generically dependent continuant on the ground that the same obligation can be concretized in many documents and survives the loss of any one of them; or under specifically dependent continuant, with a stated rationale. Either is acceptable if argued.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
The reviewer can identify, for every top-level legal class, its BFO placement and the reason for it, and checks it against the LOF design patterns.

Automated check: None. Manual review.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every entity has a persistent IRI in the https://w3id.org/lof/ namespace, and IRIs are never reassigned or deleted.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal data annotated with an ontology term must mean the same thing years later. Identifiers that move, change meaning, or disappear silently corrupt every dataset that uses them.

  2. Local identifiers are opaque and never encode the label.
  3. A term whose meaning changes gets a new IRI, and the old term is deprecated following the deprecation policy.
  4. Terms are never deleted from the ontology.

docs.title: Summary

docs.title: Purpose

docs.title: LOF-P-007: Textual definitions
docs.text:
Proposed for adoption

This principle is part of a proposal for adoption, Adopt principles: terms: identifiers, definitions, and names (#56), which is not yet open for decision. Comments are welcome now, from anyone. When it opens, members will be able to approve or object here.

comment without GitHub · comment on GitHub

Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every class and relation has a precise, non-circular textual definition.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: In law, the meaning of a term is often the point in dispute. Definitions make the intended meaning checkable by lawyers and domain experts who will never read an axiom.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Every class and relation in the ontology's namespace has exactly one English definition, recorded with skos:definition or IAO:0000115.
  2. Class definitions take genus and differentia form where possible: "An X is a Y that Z", where Y is the asserted parent.
  3. Definitions do not use the term being defined, and cite a source (statute, case, treatise) with dcterms:source where one exists.
  4. Textual and logical definitions agree. Where a class also has a logical definition (an equivalence axiom, or subclass axioms giving necessary conditions), the textual definition states the same conditions in words, and the logical definition formalizes them: the genus is the same class in both, and each condition in one appears in the other. Conditions that OWL cannot express (for example, about time or about what an agent intends) are stated in the textual definition and noted in an rdfs:comment beginning "Not expressed in OWL:". The textual definition records the intended meaning; if the two diverge, the axioms are corrected to match it, or the term is redefined as a new term (LOF-P-005).

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Add the definition when the term is created. Protégé's annotation panel supports both properties.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: legal role: "A role that inheres in a person or organization in virtue of recognition by a legal institution and that is realized in legally significant processes." (Illustrative only.)

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Definitions are present, match the asserted parent, agree with the logical definition where there is one, and are intelligible to a legal expert.

Automated check: SPARQL check missing-definition-violation.

docs.title: LOF-P-009: Orthogonality
docs.text:
Proposed for adoption

This principle is part of a proposal for adoption, Adopt principles: scope and coordination (#57), which is not yet open for decision. Comments are welcome now, from anyone. When it opens, members will be able to approve or object here.

comment without GitHub · comment on GitHub

Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Member ontologies do not duplicate one another's content.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Two classes for the same legal entity, minted in two ontologies, force every user to reconcile them. Orthogonality means each kind of entity is defined once, by the group best placed to maintain it.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Before minting a term, developers check the registry for an existing member-ontology term with the same meaning.
  2. Where one exists, it is imported or referenced by IRI rather than redefined.
  3. Overlaps found in review are resolved by the maintainers concerned, with the Editorial Working Group mediating.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Import the relevant module from the other member ontology through the catalog, as the template does for BFO.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: An ontology of court procedure reuses legal role from a roles ontology rather than defining its own judge role parent class.

docs.title: Criteria for review

docs.title: LOF-P-010: Jurisdictional transparency
docs.text:
Proposed for adoption

This principle is part of a proposal for adoption, Adopt principles: legal specificity (#58), which is not yet open for decision. Comments are welcome now, from anyone. When it opens, members will be able to approve or object here.

comment without GitHub · comment on GitHub

Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Classes specific to a legal system or jurisdiction carry a dcterms:coverage annotation naming it, and are not presented as universal.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal categories vary across systems. A class that silently generalizes from one jurisdiction ("consideration" in common-law contract, say) misrepresents others and produces false inferences when data from several systems is combined.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. The registry entry lists the jurisdictions or legal traditions in scope (jurisdictions), or general if the ontology claims generality.
  2. Classes restricted to particular jurisdictions carry a dcterms:coverage annotation naming them.
  3. Claims of cross-jurisdictional generality are supported by documentation.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Mark each such class with one dcterms:coverage annotation per jurisdiction or tradition, using these values:

Scope Value Example A country ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code "BR" (Brazil) A subdivision (state, province) ISO 3166-2 code "US-TX" (Texas) The European Union "EU" "EU" A legal tradition one of common-law, civil-law, religious-law, customary-law, international-law "common-law"

A class with no dcterms:coverage annotation is presented as general, so the annotation is required, not optional, for every class whose definition depends on a particular legal system.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A class consideration annotated with dcterms:coverage "common-law".

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Jurisdiction-specific classes are annotated. The ontology's generality claims are plausible given its sources.

Automated check: none yet; a check of dcterms:coverage values against the table above is planned. Whether a class needs the annotation remains a matter for manual review.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Each release is logically consistent and contains no unsatisfiable classes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: An inconsistent ontology entails everything, and an unsatisfiable class can have no instances. Either defect makes automated reasoning over legal data worthless.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. The ontology, merged with its imports, is consistent under an OWL 2 DL reasoner (HermiT, or ELK for large EL ontologies).
  2. No named class is unsatisfiable.
  3. The check passes before every release.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: make test runs the HermiT check through ROBOT. CI runs it on every push and pull request.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: See the LOF ontology template.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
CI is green on the release commit.

Automated check: robot reason in CI.

docs.text:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Labels are unique, singular, and follow a consistent lexical style.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Consistent labels make ontologies readable together and reduce errors when terms are chosen from pick lists.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Every entity has exactly one rdfs:label per language.
  2. Labels are singular nouns or noun phrases, in lower case except for proper nouns and established acronyms.
  3. Labels are unique within the ontology, and preferably within the Foundry.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Use skos:altLabel for synonyms and jurisdiction-specific alternative names rather than adding a second label.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: "legal obligation", not "Legal Obligations"; "European Court of Human Rights" keeps its capitals.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Label style is consistent, and warnings from the label-case check are justified.

Automated check: SPARQL checks missing-label-violation, multiple-labels-violation, and the label-uppercase-warning report; ROBOT report check duplicate_label.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Maintainers respond to issues and keep the ontology aligned with its dependencies.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal ontologies must track changes in law and in the ontologies they import. An unmaintained ontology gradually becomes wrong.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Maintainers respond to new issues within 30 days.
  2. The ontology is updated to the current release of BFO and of any member ontology it imports within a reasonable period of their release.
  3. An ontology whose maintainers cannot continue is marked orphaned in the registry, and the coordinators seek new maintainers.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Watch the repositories of imported ontologies, and schedule periodic make imports refreshes.

docs.text: See the LOF ontology template.

docs.text:
Issue response history and the date of the last import refresh.

docs.text:

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology documents its relationship to established legal information standards.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal information already circulates in established formats. Documented mappings let Foundry ontologies annotate that data rather than compete with it.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Where a relevant standard exists (for example Akoma Ntoso, LegalRuleML, LKIF, ELI, ECLI), the README states whether and how the ontology maps to it.
  2. Term-level mappings, where provided, use skos:exactMatch, skos:closeMatch, skos:broadMatch, or skos:narrowMatch, or a SSSOM mapping file.
  3. Mappings are not asserted as logical equivalences unless the ontological commitments have been checked.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Keep mappings in a separate SSSOM file under src/mappings/ when they are numerous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A class for judgments mapped to the Akoma Ntoso judgment document type with skos:closeMatch.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Relevant standards are identified, and mappings use the appropriate SKOS strength.

docs.title: LOF-P-018: Attribution
docs.text:
Proposed for adoption

This principle is part of a proposal for adoption, Adopt principles: openness and credit (#54), which is not yet open for decision. Comments are welcome now, from anyone. When it opens, members will be able to approve or object here.

comment without GitHub · comment on GitHub

Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Contributors to the ontology are credited, and the ontology, each of its releases, and the contributions to it can be cited.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Ontology development is scholarly work. Credit sustains contributions, and citability lets that work count in the academic and professional record.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. The ontology header lists creators with dcterms:creator and contributors with dcterms:contributor, using ORCID IRIs where available.
  2. Term-level contributions may be recorded with dcterms:contributor on the term.
  3. The README gives a preferred citation of the ontology, naming its creators, title, version, and version IRI (LOF-P-006), so that each release can be cited exactly. A DOI for each release (for example, through Zenodo) is recommended.
  4. Contributions are citable through the release that contains them: a term's dcterms:contributor records who contributed it, and the term's IRI and the release's version IRI identify it, so a contribution can be cited as "term, contributor, ontology, version". The repository history records the same contributions in detail.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Add ORCID IRIs to the header when onboarding each new contributor.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Annotation(dcterms:creator <https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000>)

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Creators are listed, contributors are credited where they contributed terms, and a citation of the current release is given.

Automated check: None. Manual review.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
Ontologies and design patterns registered with the Foundry. Status values are defined in the metadata policy. Machine-readable versions: ontologies.yml, ontologies.jsonld.

ID Title Prefix Jurisdictions Status Activity nao Normative Accountability Ontology (NAO) NAO general draft active odp-001 LOF-ODP-001: Legal Act and Legal Document ODP001 general draft active odp-002 LOF-ODP-002: Legal Role Conferral ODP002 general draft active odp-003 LOF-ODP-003: Correlative Deontic Positions ODP003 general draft active odp-004 LOF-ODP-004: Minimum Legal Chain ODP004 general draft active odp-005 LOF-ODP-005: Legal Time and Versions ODP005 general draft active odp-006 LOF-ODP-006: Relations between Norms ODP006 general draft active

To register an ontology, follow the new ontology request SOP.

docs.title: SOP: New ontology request
docs.text:
1. Check the registry. Make sure no existing ontology already covers the scope (LOF-P-009).
  2. Open a request. Use the New ontology request issue form in the website repository. You will be asked for a title, requested prefix, scope statement, competency questions, jurisdictions, planned use, and contact.
  3. Scope discussion. An Editorial Working Group member responds, usually within 30 days, checking for overlap and agreeing the prefix.
  4. Register at draft status. Once scope and prefix are agreed, open a pull request adding ontology/{id}.md with status: draft. A coordinator merges it. The prefix is now reserved, and the w3id.org/lof redirects are regenerated.
  5. Create the repository. Create lof-{id} in the Foundry organization (or link your own), and initialize it from the ontology template with ./init.sh.
  6. Develop. Follow the principles. Keep CI green.
  7. Request review. When ready, follow the review SOP.

docs.title: SOP: Release
docs.text:
In the ontology repository:

  1. Make sure CI is green on main.
  2. Update CHANGELOG.md with the new version and date.
  3. From src/ontology/, run make release VERSION=x.y.z. This regenerates lof-{id}.owl and lof-{id}-base.owl at the repository root, with version IRI and version info set.
  4. Commit the release files and changelog: git commit -am "Release x.y.z".
  5. Tag and push: git tag vx.y.z && git push && git push --tags.
  6. Optionally, create a GitHub release from the tag.
  7. Check that https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/releases/x.y.z/{id}.owl resolves.

Use semantic versioning (LOF-P-006): PATCH for corrections to labels and definitions, MINOR for new terms, MAJOR for changes that can alter inferences over existing data.

docs.title: SOP: Ontology review
docs.text:
Review moves an ontology from candidate to accepted.

  1. Submit. The contact person opens a pull request changing the ontology's status to candidate, linking a tagged release.
  2. Assign reviewers. The Editorial Working Group assigns two reviewers: one Operations Committee member and one reviewer who is not a maintainer of the ontology.
  3. Review. Each reviewer opens an Ontology review issue using the form, which lists every principle as a checkbox, and records findings for each unmet principle. Automated check results are taken from the ontology's CI.
  4. Revise. Maintainers address findings and tag a new release. Reviewers update their issues.
  5. Decide. When both reviewers recommend acceptance, the change to status: accepted is approved as a substantive change (see Governance), and the review field records the date and issue.

docs.title: Re-review
docs.text: Accepted ontologies are re-reviewed if a principle is amended in a way that affects them, or if an overlap dispute is raised.

docs.title: SOP: Term requests
docs.text:
Anyone may request a new term, or a change to an existing term, in any member ontology.

  1. Open an issue in the ontology's tracker (https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/tracker) using the New term request form. Give a proposed label, definition, parent class, source, and an example of use.
  2. A maintainer responds within 30 days (LOF-P-014), either adding the term, pointing to an existing term, or explaining why it is out of scope.
  3. If the term belongs in a different member ontology, the maintainer transfers the issue there.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Tools for seeing and checking ontologies before you propose them to the Foundry. All are free. The two marked † were built by a founding coordinator, David Koepsell.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
Tool What it is When to use it owl2uml † Web app that draws an OWL file as a UML class diagram To see the shape of a pattern or a small ontology at a glance: drop the file in, no installation. WebVOWL Web app that draws an ontology as an interactive graph (VOWL notation) To explore a larger ontology interactively, or to show its structure to non-ontologists. Protégé Desktop ontology editor, with class-hierarchy and graph views To edit an ontology and browse its hierarchy, and as the usual home for running a reasoner by hand.

The design pattern pages also carry a diagram of each pattern, drawn automatically from the pattern's tables every time the site is built.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Tool What it is When to use it OwlTester † Web app that checks an OWL file against BFO and common modeling errors, in plain language For a quick first check of BFO conformance before asking anyone to review, no installation. HermiT OWL 2 DL reasoner (built into Protégé and ROBOT) To check that an ontology is consistent and has no unsatisfiable classes (principle LOF-P-011), and to see what follows from its axioms. ROBOT Command-line tool from the OBO community for reasoning, quality reports, SPARQL checks, extracts, and releases For the Foundry's automated checks and for building releases; this is what the Foundry's own checks run. pySHACL Python validator for SHACL shapes To check instance data (worked examples, test cases) against shapes, with messages written for people rather than reasoner output.
